families.s: HSE management of excessive and insufficient workload
families.t: information processing, memory, decisions, task demand, underload, peaks, staffing, competence and job satisfaction
f: People have limited capacity to process information, retain items in memory, make decisions and perform tasks.
Excess workload can slow performance and increase slips, lapses and mistakes.
Insufficient workload can cause boredom, loss of situation awareness and reduced alertness.
Workload can become especially significant during downsizing, incidents, turnarounds and other peaks.
Workload is related to competence, working hours, organisational change and staffing levels.
Experienced personnel may require less conscious processing for familiar tasks than inexperienced personnel.
High or perceived high workload can reduce job satisfaction and contribute to turnover and staff shortages.
Work design should balance task demands, time, interruptions, information, staffing and individual capability.
families.g: Information processing, memory, decisions, task demand, underload, peaks, staffing, competence and job satisfaction guidance is general organisational and human-factors evidence and does not prove current staffing, competence, behaviour, controls, performance or exact risk at an individual parcel.

families.t: responsibilities, workload, emergency roles, permits, contractors, work allocation, monitoring, leadership and workforce involvement
f: Supervision is an important performance-influencing factor and has contributed to major accidents when inadequate.
Problems can arise from poorly defined responsibilities, heavy workloads, inadequate resources or removing supervisory roles.
Supervisors with emergency-response duties need suitable training and competence.
Supervisors may have important roles in contractor management and permit-to-work systems.
Supervisory functions include planning and allocating work.
Supervisors make decisions and monitor performance and compliance.
Supervisors provide leadership, build teamwork and support workforce involvement.
Effective supervision can improve procedure compliance, competence, communication, staffing, workload and safety culture.

families.s: HSE human-factors controls for contractor management
families.t: selection, client knowledge, coordination, induction, supervision, competence, subcontractors and completed-work verification
f: Contractors may replace or supplement company staff and may provide services on-site or elsewhere.
Using contractors does not remove the client's need to understand the supplied product or service and manage safe operations.
Contractor selection should consider resources, equipment, knowledge and experience.
Clients, contractors and subcontractors should coordinate who does what, when and how.
Contractors need induction to site rules, procedures, hazards and emergency arrangements.
Supervision arrangements should identify who provides on-the-job oversight.
Contractor competence should be considered at both worker and management level.
Checks of completed work and safe handback should form part of contractor control.

families.s: HSE safety-critical spoken and written communications
families.t: risk information, induction, emergency messages, team coordination, contractors, lifting, confined spaces, handover and permits
f: Spoken and written communication can be critical to maintaining safety.
Safety information may need to pass within teams, between teams and during operations, maintenance and emergencies.
Employees, contractors and visitors should have access to information needed to negotiate workplace hazards safely.
Relevant information can include risk-assessment findings, site induction, emergency instructions and safety warnings.
Communication is safety-critical in activities such as lifting, emergency response and confined-space entry.
Different parties and organisations should coordinate activities through clear communication.
Shift handover is a key form of safety-critical communication.
A permit-to-work is a communication mechanism linking management, supervisors, operators and the people performing work.

families.s: HSE reliable shift and task handover
families.t: preparation, face-to-face exchange, task-relevant information, cross-checking, responsibility, maintenance, records and continuity
f: Handover is needed when tasks and responsibilities pass to another person, shift or function.
The goal is accurate and reliable communication of task-relevant information so safe work continues.
Effective handover includes preparation by outgoing personnel.
Outgoing and incoming personnel should exchange relevant information during the handover.
Incoming personnel should cross-check information as they assume responsibility.
Communication failures at shift handover have contributed to serious accidents.
Planned maintenance work is a recurring context in handover-related incidents.
Time, suitable records and an opportunity for questions should be provided for safety-critical handover.
